banner: It records the positions the board proposes and resolves, with who proposed each one. It does not recommend what the board's position should be. Questions about the company's legal obligations are recorded for counsel to answer.

modes.name: Standalone
modes.for: Companies outside prudential regulation. The steps produce the whole appetite.

modes.name: Connected
modes.for: APRA, ASIC or MAS regulated entities. The steps produce board directions that the AI Risk Appetite engagement must stay within.

steps.name: Set-up and pre-read
steps.question: What applies to us, and what do directors need to know first?
steps.answeredAs: Scope, mode, privilege position, matter brief

steps.name: Where AI is used
steps.question: What AI do we use now, directly and through providers?
steps.answeredAs: An inventory of 10 to 20 lines, each with authority level and the automated-decision flag

steps.name: Posture
steps.question: Where do we want AI to create value, and how cautious are we in each area?
steps.answeredAs: A posture, Avoid to Pursue, for each area of the business
prompts: Where would AI most help our people or customers? Where would we least want to see it?
Is there an area where a mistake by AI would be hard to explain to customers or staff?
Does any area already use AI beyond the posture we are about to set? (Compare with B1.)
Are we content for providers to use AI in an area where we would not use it ourselves?
steps.start: The current state: each area starts at the posture that matches the highest authority the inventory records there. The board confirms or changes it.

steps.name: Red lines
steps.question: Which uses of AI do we not accept at all?
steps.answeredAs: A list of uses, each testable against the inventory
prompts: Is there anything we would stop at once if we found it in the inventory?
Is there a decision about a person we would never let AI make alone?
Is there information that must never reach any AI tool?
Would we accept a provider doing something we have ruled out for ourselves?
steps.start: None. A list of uses boards commonly consider is shown only if the board asks. Its inclusion is not a recommendation.

steps.name: Reserved to the board
steps.question: Which AI decisions must come back to us?
steps.answeredAs: A list of events, each with who brings it and when
prompts: At what authority level do we want to approve a use before it starts?
What can the CEO approve alone, and must it be reported?
How quickly must we hear of an exception?
steps.start: The six events RV1 to RV6, with the authority level in RV1, before or after, and who brings each left for the session.

steps.name: Confidential information
steps.question: What information may go into which AI tools?
steps.answeredAs: Permitted, with conditions, or not permitted, for each class and tool kind
prompts: What do our existing confidentiality, privacy and acceptable-use policies already say? We start there.
Would we know if a board paper were pasted into a chatbot on a phone?
Do our advisers’ engagement letters say anything about their AI tools?
Does a ban move the use somewhere we cannot see?
steps.start: What existing policies already say. Cells no policy covers are left for the session.

steps.name: Harm we will not tolerate
steps.question: What failure would be unacceptable to customers, staff or the company?
steps.answeredAs: A statement and a threshold for each kind of harm
prompts: Do we already have thresholds for incidents, losses or complaints? If so, we use them unchanged.
Does one person wrongly treated count, or does it take a pattern?
Which operations could an AI failure, ours or a provider’s, stop?
steps.start: Existing incident, loss and complaint thresholds, unchanged. A new threshold is set only where none exists.

steps.name: What we expect to hear
steps.question: What should management report to us about AI, and how fast?
steps.answeredAs: Three to six measures, and the events reported between meetings
prompts: Which three to five numbers would tell us whether AI is being used as we intend?
What must reach the chair before the next meeting, and how fast?
How does a member of staff, a customer or a provider raise a concern about our use of AI, and how do we hear of it?
steps.start: The six measures BM1 to BM6 and four events EV1 to EV4, with limits, owners and times left for the session. BM6 counts concerns about AI that people raise (ISO/IEC 42001:2023, A.3.3).

steps.name: Who is accountable
steps.question: Which committee, director and executive own AI?
steps.answeredAs: A named owner for the whole and for each area
prompts: Does AI sit with the audit and risk committee, the full board, or a new committee?
Is the accountable executive the one closest to the technology, or to the risk?
In connected mode: does the AI owner match the accountability map, and the accountable persons under it?
steps.start: The existing committee charter and delegations.

steps.name: Resolve and review
steps.question: Do we resolve this, and when do we look again?
steps.answeredAs: A resolution, a review interval and change events

toolKind.K1: An enterprise assistant that can answer from the company’s own stored files and email, within each person’s access.
toolKind.K2: A licensed AI tool the company has approved, which works on what a person types or uploads.
toolKind.K3: AI inside meeting and collaboration tools: transcription, recaps and AI notetakers.
toolKind.K4: A consumer AI tool, not approved by the company, opened in the browser on a company device.
toolKind.K5: AI on a personal phone or computer, outside the company’s controls.
toolKind.K7: An adviser’s own AI tools: the bank, law firm or consultant working for the company.

ref.L: A line in the AI inventory (step B1): one AI use the company has now.
ref.RL: A red line (step B3): a use of AI the board does not accept at all.
ref.RV: A decision reserved to the board (step B4): it comes back to the board before or after it happens.
ref.BM: A board measure (step B7): reported to the board at each meeting.
ref.EV: An event (step B7) that must reach the board between meetings, within the time shown.
ref.QC: A question to counsel: a legal point logged for the GC to answer, not settled in the room.
ref.GL: A governance goal (step B2): what the board wants AI governance to achieve, with an owner and a measure B7 reports.

tips.adm: Whether this AI makes, or substantially contributes to, a decision about a person using their personal information. Australia’s Privacy Act requires these to be described in the privacy policy from 10 December 2026; counsel decides what that means for each line.
tips.reality: Inventory lines that already go past a position the board has set. They are not failures: each one becomes an action on the 90-day list, so the board takes its positions knowing what they mean today.
tips.recorded: Something has been recorded for this step.
tips.notYet: Nothing has been recorded for this step yet.
tips.notSet: Not set: the room could not settle this position. It is recorded with who will set it and by when, so nothing is left blank.

managementBriefing.title: Management briefing
managementBriefing.tip: The meeting with the CIO or AI lead and the AI governance team, held before anything goes to directors. It sets out what the board will decide, what it will not, and how the inventory is used.
managementBriefing.intro: The board advisor, the GC and Triodian meet the technology owner and the AI governance team before anything reaches directors. The inventory is theirs to bring.
managementBriefing.notYet: Record the meeting here once it is held. Where the company has no separate technology lead, record that with the reason.
managementBriefing.noRoles: No one has the technology owner or AI governance team role yet. Give the roles in Admin, or record why the briefing is not needed.
managementBriefing.status: Drafted by Triodian for the board advisor, and settled by the GC before it is issued. It is not legal advice.

p: How far AI may go in each area of the business, the uses it will not accept, the decisions it keeps for itself, what may be put into which kind of tool, the harm it will not tolerate, and what it wants reported. Each position is proposed by a director, the chair or the CEO, and recorded with who proposed it.

sections.h: What the board will not decide
p: Which tools to buy, how they are built or configured, or how the technology function is run. Those stay with management. The board does not review individual deployments in this engagement.

The AI governance team enters and maintains the list of AI in use, and the technology owner confirms each line. The board reads it to test each position against what is in use today: a posture against the highest authority recorded in the area, and each red line against the lines it would cross.
Existing policies and thresholds are brought the same way, so the board starts from what the company has already set.

sections.h: Where a use is already past a position
p: A use that goes beyond a position the board takes is not a finding on a past decision. It becomes an action on the 90-day list, with an owner and a date, and the list goes to the CEO with the board behind it.
The AI governance team drafts the measures the board will receive at each meeting, and the technology owner confirms each. A director or the CEO proposes them to the board.
A written record of what the CEO can approve alone and what goes to the board, the measures, a named person for each accountability, and the 90-day action list.

briefing.title: Director briefing
briefing.intro: Every director starts the workshop from the same place. This briefing takes about fifteen minutes: AI in plain terms, the obligations in scope for the company, how directors’ duties bear on AI, and the ways AI commonly fails. It ends with four questions that check understanding. They are not a test, and no one else on the board sees your answers.
briefing.status: Drafted by Triodian for the board advisor, and settled by the GC before it is issued. It is not legal advice.

p: In this engagement, AI means software that produces text, scores, recommendations, decisions or actions from patterns in data, rather than from rules a person wrote out. It includes tools staff use directly, such as chat assistants and meeting notes, and the AI that providers use in the work they do for the company.

What matters to the board is less how the technology works than what it is allowed to do. The framework puts that on one scale, from Assists (a person still acts) to Changes systems (the AI holds credentials to change systems unattended). Much of the risk sits in the step from Recommends to Decides: the point at which no person reviews the output before it takes effect.

AI can be wrong in ways that look right. It can state things that are not true, treat similar people differently, pass on information it was given, or behave differently after its provider updates it. None of these needs a fault in the company’s own systems.

The board oversees AI in the way it oversees the rest of the business: by setting direction, knowing what is in use, and expecting to hear when something goes wrong. Directors do not need to understand how a model works. They need to know where AI is used, what it is allowed to do, and who answers for it.

What directors’ duties require of this board in relation to AI, and whether any obligation in scope calls for a board-level position, are questions for counsel. The GC will brief the board on them before the workshop. Nothing in this briefing says what the law requires.

list: A customer is given wrong information by a chatbot and relies on it.
An applicant or customer is screened out by a scoring tool no one reviews.
A board paper or price-sensitive document is pasted into a public chatbot.
A provider changes the AI behind a service without telling the company.
An automated payment or order runs on a wrong figure, again and again, before anyone notices.
Staff use unapproved AI tools because the approved ones do not meet their needs.

briefing.obligationsNote: From the AI Obligations Atlas matter brief. The tiers describe sources, not what applies: Binding is law or a prudential standard in force; Expected is regulator guidance or a recognised standard; Anticipated is made but not yet in force, or under consultation. Counsel decides what applies to the company.
briefing.checksIntro: A check of understanding, not a test. Choose an answer to see the explanation. Only you and the facilitators (the board advisor and Triodian) see your answers.

checks.q: An AI tool shortlists job applicants and a recruiter decides whom to interview. Which authority level is that?
checks.why: The AI ranks and a person decides, so it is Recommends (A2). It would be Decides (A3) if no person reviewed the shortlist before it took effect.

checks.q: Which posture accepts AI that decides within stated limits, where the board can see what it did?
checks.why: Open (S3). Cautious accepts AI that assists or recommends, with a person deciding. Pursue accepts less oversight, within the red lines and reserved decisions.

checks.q: In the workshop, who proposes where a position is set?
options: The board advisor or the GC
A director, the chair or the CEO
checks.why: Positions come from the board and management. The board advisor, the GC and Triodian explain, answer questions and record.

checks.q: A director asks whether the company must tell customers about a decision AI made. What happens in the workshop?
options: The room settles it and moves on
It is logged as a question to counsel
checks.why: Anything that turns on what the company is obliged to do is logged as a numbered question to counsel, and not settled in the room.

harm.title: Harm kinds H1 to H6 beside ISO/IEC 42001:2023 A.5 and ISO/IEC 42005:2025
harm.intro: ISO/IEC 42005:2025 describes an AI system impact assessment: the impact of one AI system on individuals, on groups of individuals and on society, across its life cycle. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 asks for it in clause 6.1.4 and controls A.5.2 to A.5.5. The board’s harm thresholds (B6) are not that assessment. They say what harm the board will not tolerate, and so what a later impact assessment is measured against. Three of the six kinds are harm to the company itself, which is a matter for risk assessment (clause 6.1.2), not impact assessment.

fastPathNote: Baseline control BC2. Management approves a new AI use that assists or recommends (A1 or A2) and reaches no threshold the board set at B6 within the number of days set here, and reports it under BM1. Anything above that goes to the reserved events. A quick approved route moves AI use onto sanctioned tools; BM7 and BM8 show whether it does.
